system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one into the fixed
template below so that a reader cannot tell what field, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, nor what
kind of work it is: an experiment, a new procedure, a measurement suite, a write-up choice, or a decision about what
to share or fund must all read alike. Keep the trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

Template, one entry per item:
- "situation": one sentence, at most 30 words: the position the researcher was in when the decision came up.
- "options_considered": two or three short options separated by " / ", including the one taken. If the source names
  no alternative, give the plain opposite of what was done.
- "choice": one sentence, at most 25 words, starting with "Chose", saying which option was taken.
- "reason": one sentence, at most 25 words, giving the stated reason; if none is stated write "No reason stated."

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, procedures, organisations, people,
  papers and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area.
- Use only plain generic words such as: the result, the claim, the finding, the check, the comparison, the setup,
  the change, the next step, the question, the work, the variant, the condition, the sample, the system.
- Never use any of these words or any form of them: ability, access, accuracy, allow, appeared, assessment, attack, avoid, baselines, behavior, behaviour, benchmark, best, bound, call, capability, cheap, claiming, clean, comes, complex, components, content, cost, defense, difficulty, disclosure, effect, effects, error, evaluate, evaluated, evaluating, evaluation, evaluator, evaluators, failures, features, form, format, four, gains, generalise, generalization, generalize, ground, harm, harmful, implication, improve, improvement, information, internal, intervention, judged, key, limit, matched, mechanism, method, methods, metric, observed, organisation, pattern, performance, phenomenon, picture, point, policy, possibly, practical, preference, preferences, public, publication, publish, rater, reduce, release, residual, responses, risk, rule, safety, sampled, say, score, shifts, similar, source, stage, success, supporting, task, tasks, technique, time, tool, tools, trait, transfer, transferred, treatment, unintended, unmodified, unwanted, value, varies, verify, wording.
- Add nothing that is not in the source. Never say who made the decision. Write every item in the same plain style.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "situation": ..., "options_considered": ..., "choice": ..., "reason": ...}, ...]}
with one entry per input item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:9879e6515ddd",
  "problem": "Whether agent results are sensitive to analysis choices such as binarizing scores or uneven task-family sizes.",
  "did": "They ran ablations using average continuous scores instead of binarized success, and a family-size weighted average using the inverse square root of family size.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "binarizing via success thresholds",
   "unweighted averaging across tasks"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Task families with more tasks might bias or skew results, and continuous scores give higher resolution signal."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:2c485213a28a",
  "problem": "Whether attacks learned against one accessible model carry over to other models.",
  "did": "They trained on individual models, such as the open-weight GPT-oss-20b alone, and measured how the attacks transferred to the other targets.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "optimizing a weighted sum of rewards across multiple models"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Training on less robust models may give a useful intermediate signal for attacking more robust ones."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:a410db4d205e",
  "problem": "How strongly to interpret the LLM-as-a-Judge's strong average performance as evidence for the method.",
  "did": "They cautioned against reading the results as an endorsement of relying solely on LLM judges, since the judge fails on lies that depend on private knowledge and fact-checking.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The HP-KR truthfulness hinges on the assistant's actual knowledge, which is hard for an external judge to infer, and future judges may not fact-check reliably."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:7fe32db45777",
  "problem": "How closely clean data must match the poison",
  "did": "Replaced the clean data with Alpaca, Open-Platypus, CodeAlpaca-20k and GSM8K, and with other kinds of bird names",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "Alpaca",
   "Open-Platypus",
   "CodeAlpaca-20k",
   "GSM8K",
   "modern names for the same birds"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To test how closely the clean examples must match the poisoned data to trigger homeopathic learning."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:70e85a3b92ca",
  "problem": "Whether IAs can surface behaviors already present in the base model on which the IA was trained, not just those introduced by fine-tuning.",
  "did": "They trained an IA on an AuditBench model as the base using only Harmful and Backdoor categories, then tested it on that base model for two adversarially robust, out-of-distribution AuditBench behaviors never trained for.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "To test whether IAs can improve more generic introspective capabilities in the model itself."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:e7d172489e8f",
  "problem": "How to measure whether an end-to-end oversight assistant is actually working.",
  "did": "They proposed grounding assistant quality in whether humans who interacted with it can accurately answer probing questions about the overseen system.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Oversight assistants ultimately provide information to humans, so quality should be tied to how well that information supports human understanding."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:1b346ea949d3",
  "problem": "What evidence to collect to detect sabotage transfer",
  "did": "Used Bloom multi-turn audits with an LLM judge (polite vs rude user, 12 scenarios, 720 audits per model per condition), plus a separate fixed-prompt evaluation with no auditor",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "fixed-prompt evaluation without an auditor model"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Some Bloom-flagged sabotage may just be the model reversing its safe advice to accommodate a dissatisfied user, so a controlled fixed-prompt evaluation with a neutral safe/unsafe choice was added"
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:4db1a61a81db",
  "problem": "How to compare agents against humans given large variance across human attempts and sources.",
  "did": "They cautioned against comparing to the average human result and argued that comparison to the most successful human attempts is more suitable.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "comparing against the average human result"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Human results vary widely, and different baseliner sources differ significantly (0.96 vs 0.46 average), while the risk question concerns researchers at their best."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:7a16df44a39c",
  "problem": "How to prevent the jailbreak investigator from reward hacking by satisfying the affirmative-prefix target without producing actually harmful output.",
  "did": "They augmented the DPO reward with a Llama-3.1 8B harmfulness judge and also required the next token not be EOS.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "targeting only the affirmative response string"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To alleviate reward hacking, i.e. to check that responses are actually harmful."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:fa713e31e1c1",
  "problem": "Whether to count a tailored many-shot jailbreaking prompt that worked better on SSC as a legitimate result.",
  "did": "Rejected the tailored SSC prompt and kept the generic fixed prompt for the benchmark, reporting MSJ as largely ineffective.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "a tailored prompt with examples of decoding other Base64-encoded constraints"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The tailored setup assumes the auditor already knows how to construct and decode such constraints, which is unrealistic."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:2e6efd5adf85",
  "problem": "How to isolate the gap between attacking CTF-like code and attacking real-world code.",
  "did": "The authors added 24 simplified CTF-like re-implementations of real defenses from the Google self-study course as a comparison subset next to the real-world repositories.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "evaluating only real-world repositories"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Because the CTF defenses are re-writes of actual literature defenses, they permit a direct comparison between CTF-like and real-world defenses."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:54bba9979508",
  "problem": "How strongly to claim that the earlier pre-deployment work amounted to oversight or accountability.",
  "did": "METR declined to claim it had audited the models, pointing to the NDA terms and the absence of any formal link to deployment decisions.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Under the NDA METR had no right or responsibility to disclose findings, and no formal expectation existed that the work would inform deployment decisions."
 }
]
